scenes.visual: Title card 'Weighing the Drain' over a mesh bag of leaves lying on a forest floor beside a balance. Same COLOUR MAP (both films): producers GREEN (the oak), consumers ORANGE (deer, mouse, fox), decomposers PURPLE (fungus threads, bacteria dots), matter = small GOLD dots inside leaves, soil and air, energy = one YELLOW wavy arrow. The leaf pile sits inside a pale BLUE-GREY bathtub outline drawn across the forest floor. Flat cartoon style; anything not measured is labelled 'schematic'. Added for this film: the higher site's data in BLUE dots and line.

scenes.tts: The first film showed decomposers draining the leaf pile. But how fast does a real forest's drain run? How could you measure matter you cannot see leaving?
scenes.visual: Quick recap tile: the BLUE-GREY bathtub with GOLD dots rising out as carbon dioxide and sinking as nutrients (as in film 1). A stopwatch icon and the words 'how fast?' appear over the PURPLE drain.
scenes.narration: The first film showed decomposers draining the leaf pile. But how fast does a real forest's drain run? How could you measure matter you cannot see leaving?

scenes.tts: Researchers in West Virginia found a way. In October twenty eleven, they worked in the Weimer Run watershed, near the town of Davis.
scenes.caption: Researchers in West Virginia found a way. In October 2011, they worked in the Weimer Run watershed, near the town of Davis.
scenes.visual: Simple map: Virginia and West Virginia outlines; a pin at Davis, West Virginia, label 'Weimer Run watershed'. On screen: 'October 2011'. The map zooms to a forested hillside above a small stream.
scenes.narration: Researchers in West Virginia found a way. In October 2011, they worked in the Weimer Run watershed, near the town of Davis.

scenes.tts: They sealed dried yellow birch leaves in mesh bags, and weighed the leaves first. Then they set the bags on the forest floor, at three heights above the stream.
scenes.visual: Step 1: cartoon hands seal yellow leaves into a fine mesh bag; the bag goes on a balance, readout '100%'. Step 2: bags laid at three spots on the hillside, labelled 'lower', 'middle', 'higher'. The higher spot gets a BLUE ring.
scenes.narration: They sealed dried yellow birch leaves in mesh bags, and weighed the leaves first. Then they set the bags on the forest floor, at three heights above the stream.

scenes.tts: Five times over two years, they brought some bags back. Different bags came back each time. They dried the leaves and weighed them again.
scenes.visual: A calendar strip runs along the bottom with five ticks: months 1, 8, 12, 20, 24. At each tick a hand lifts a different bag from the hillside. Step 3: leaves into a drying oven icon, then onto the balance.
scenes.narration: Five times over two years, they brought some bags back. Different bags came back each time. They dried the leaves and weighed them again.

scenes.tts: Why dry the leaves before weighing? Wet leaves are heavier. Drying them means that water in the leaves does not change the result.
scenes.visual: Two balances side by side: a soggy leaf pile with water droplets reads heavier; the same leaves after drying read lower. A tick appears over the dry one: 'weigh only dry leaves'.
scenes.narration: Why dry the leaves before weighing? Wet leaves are heavier. Drying them means that water in the leaves does not change the result.

scenes.tts: Let's follow the higher site. The graph shows the percent of the starting mass left. Every bag started at one hundred percent. Each later dot is an average of eight or nine bags. After one month, about seventy-two percent was left.
scenes.caption: Let's follow the higher site. The graph shows the percent of the starting mass left. Every bag started at 100 percent. Each later dot is an average of 8 or 9 bags. After one month, about 72 percent was left.
scenes.visual: Axes draw in: y 'mass left (%)' 0 to 100, x 'months' 0 to 24. A BLUE dot at (0, 100), tagged 'start'. A second BLUE dot drops in at (1, 72.0), with the value '72.0%' on screen. Title 'higher site, Weimer Run'. Only the higher site is ever plotted in this film.
scenes.narration: Let's follow the higher site. The graph shows the percent of the starting mass left. Every bag started at 100 percent. Each later dot is an average of 8 or 9 bags. After one month, about 72 percent was left.

scenes.tts: That first drop was fast. Part of it was probably rain washing sugars and other substances out of the fresh leaves. This is called leaching. It does not need decomposers.
scenes.visual: Inset: raindrops fall on a fresh leaf; small blue-grey specks labelled 'dissolved sugars' trickle out into the soil. Label 'leaching: no decomposers needed'. The PURPLE drain icon stays dim in this inset.
scenes.narration: That first drop was fast. Part of it was probably rain washing sugars and other substances out of the fresh leaves. This is called leaching. It does not need decomposers.

scenes.tts: Now jump to twelve months. About sixty percent of the mass was left. So about forty percent was gone in one year.
scenes.caption: Now jump to 12 months. About 60 percent of the mass was left. So about 40 percent was gone in one year.
scenes.visual: The point at month 8 (68.9) appears quietly, then a BLUE dot at (12, 59.7), value '59.7%'. On screen, not spoken: '100 − 59.7 = 40.3% gone'. A bracket from 100 down to 59.7 is shaded GOLD and labelled 'gone in 1 year'.
scenes.narration: Now jump to 12 months. About 60 percent of the mass was left. So about 40 percent was gone in one year.

scenes.tts: At twenty-four months, a little under half was left. The bags were still losing mass, but more slowly than in the first year.
scenes.caption: At 24 months, a little under half was left. The bags were still losing mass, but more slowly than in the first year.
scenes.visual: Dots at (20, 55.8) and (24, 47.8) appear and the BLUE line joins all six points. Value '47.8%' at the end. A faint dashed '50%' line shows the end point just under half. The line's slope is visibly gentler in year 2; label 'slower'.
scenes.narration: At 24 months, a little under half was left. The bags were still losing mass, but more slowly than in the first year.

scenes.tts: One more thing. The mesh kept earthworms and millipedes out. On an open forest floor, would leaves break down faster or slower than in the bags?
scenes.visual: Close-up of the mesh bag: an earthworm and a millipede bump against the mesh and cannot get in. Pause-card question appears: 'Open forest floor: faster or slower?'
scenes.narration: One more thing. The mesh kept earthworms and millipedes out. On an open forest floor, would leaves break down faster or slower than in the bags?

scenes.visual: Pause card: 'Faster or slower without the mesh? Decide.' 5-second ring timer.

scenes.tts: Probably faster. Worms and millipedes tear dead leaves into smaller bits. Smaller bits give fungi and bacteria more surface to work on. So the bags probably show the drain running slower than it really does.
scenes.visual: Mesh removed: the worm and millipede shred a leaf into small pieces; PURPLE fungus threads spread over the new edges. Label 'more surface'. A ghosted line below the BLUE line is labelled 'open floor: probably faster (schematic, not measured)'.
scenes.narration: Probably faster. Worms and millipedes tear dead leaves into smaller bits. Smaller bits give fungi and bacteria more surface to work on. So the bags probably show the drain running slower than it really does.

scenes.tts: In these bags, about forty percent drained away in a year, and about half in two. Suppose a model drain took forty percent of the whole pile every year. The pile would level off near two and a half autumns' worth. But these bags lost mass more slowly in year two. So two years cannot tell us how big a real pile gets.
scenes.caption: In these bags, about 40 percent drained away in a year, and about half in two. Suppose a model drain took 40 percent of the whole pile every year. The pile would level off near 2.5 autumns' worth. But these bags lost mass more slowly in year two. So two years cannot tell us how big a real pile gets.
scenes.visual: The BLUE-GREY tub from film 1 returns, labelled 'bathtub model (schematic)'. A PURPLE drain runs with the label 'about 40% gone in year 1, about half in 2 years (higher site)'. On screen, not spoken: 'if 40% of the whole pile left every year: 1 ÷ 0.40 ≈ 2.5 autumns (model)'. The pile peaks rise and settle, labelled 'model only'. Then a small tag on the BLUE graph's year-2 stretch: 'year 2: slower', and a question mark over the real pile's height.
scenes.narration: In these bags, about 40 percent drained away in a year, and about half in two. Suppose a model drain took 40 percent of the whole pile every year. The pile would level off near 2.5 autumns' worth. But these bags lost mass more slowly in year two. So two years cannot tell us how big a real pile gets.

scenes.tts: Some early loss was probably leaching, and decomposers did some too. Weighing measures all the loss together. It cannot split decomposers from leaching or bits lost through the mesh. And it shows one kind of leaf in bags, not a whole forest floor. Weighing leaf bags measures how fast leaves lose mass.
scenes.visual: The graph and the tub sit side by side; an arrow links the falling BLUE line to the PURPLE drain. The words 'mass lost over time = all causes together (decomposers + leaching + bits through the mesh)' appear, with a small tag 'yellow birch, fine mesh bags'.
scenes.narration: Some early loss was probably leaching, and decomposers did some too. Weighing measures all the loss together. It cannot split decomposers from leaching or bits lost through the mesh. And it shows one kind of leaf in bags, not a whole forest floor. Weighing leaf bags measures how fast leaves lose mass.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. Line: 'Weighing leaf bags measures how fast leaves lose mass.'
